attributes.title: Level 4

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓Did you edit the tilemap to include orange spawn tiles that will turn into Food sprites?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ How do you add new tiles to the tilemap?

❓ Where might the Food sprites be placed on the tilemap, so that the Player sprite must jump up to reach them?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to think strategically about where they want to place the orange spawn tiles/Food sprites. Prompt them to think about how they should be spaced out and make use of the vertical design, so that the Player sprite must continue jumping up to collect all the sprites. Ask the ninja how they can design the tilemap to be both challenging and fun for the user.
steps.instructions:
Edit the tilemap to spawn Food sprites for the Player sprite to collect!


Click the square in the [set tilemap to] block to open the tilemap editor. Notice that the tilemap design is very tall.


Click “My Tiles” and select the orange tile. Place at least 6 orange tiles on the tilemap. The orange tile is a spawn tile and is setting the place for Foodsprites to be created.


Place the tiles strategically so that the Player sprite will need to continue jumping up the tilemap in order to collect all of the Food sprites. Once finished, click “Done”.

steps.hints: ❓Did you select the orange  tile in the (array of all tile locations) block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ How does the project know how many and where to place the Food sprites?

❓ How might the Player sprite reach the Food sprites located high up on the tilemap?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Walk the ninja through the sequence of the [for element] loop. In this example, for each orange spawn tile on the tilemap, the project will place an orb sprite on top of it and then make the tile blank. Because it uses the array of all orange spawn tiles, the project knows how many tiles are in the array and where they are each located on the tilemap.
steps.instructions:
Spawn Food sprites on the orange tiles.


Drag a [for element] loop into the bottom of the [on start] container. Open Scene to use an (array of all tile locations) block as the (list) value. Select the orange tile from the dropdown menu. 


Drag the Food sprite’s [set sprite to] block from the [on start] container into the [for element] loop. Then, open Scene and drag [place sprite on top of] and [set tile at] blocks into the loop. Select the Food sprite’s name, then replace the tilemap coordinates in both blocks with the (value) variable from the loop. Leave the tile blank in the [set tile at] block.


Click ▶ to see the Food sprites appear in place of the orange spawn tiles.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the Player sprite’s vy to a negative value in the [on button pressed] container?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ What might be reasonable values to use for the Player sprite’s vy and ay?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡This step enables the Player sprite to jump on the tilemap. A second [on button pressed] container with [B] selected will be added in the next step to enable the user to create new platform tiles.
steps.instructions:
Code the Player sprite to be able to jump on top of platforms and fall back down at a reasonable speed! 


In the [on button pressed] container already in the editor, add an [if then] conditional and replace the <true> value with an <is sprite hitting wall> block. Select the Player sprite’s name and [bottom] as the direction. 


Then, add a [set sprite [x]] block into the conditional and select [vy (velocity y)] from the drop down. 


Add another [set sprite [x]] block underneath the Player sprite’s blocks in the [on start] container. Use the drop down to select [ay (acceleration y)]. 


Test out different values in the vy and ay parameters, so that the Player sprite Player sprite is able to jump when touching the tilemap floor then falls to the ground at a reasonable speed.


Click ▶ to test out the project and see the Player sprite jump up and return to the ground!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you place a (tilemap location of (sprite)) block inside the (tilemap location [bottom] of (location)) block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓What will happen when the B button is pressed? 

❓How do the tilemap location blocks impact where a crate tile is set?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the B button is pressed, a crate tile will be set at the tile at the bottom of the Player sprite. This code first pulls the tilemap location at the center of the sprite, then finds the tile at the bottom of it to set the tile at.
steps.instructions:
Oh no! There are no platforms for the Player sprite to jump on! Create crate tiles below the Player sprite as it jumps to reach the Food sprites. 


Drag out another [on button pressed] container and change the button to [B]. Place a [set tile at location] block inside the container, then set a crate tile by selecting one from the drop down.


Open Scene and drag a (tilemap location [left] of (location)) block into the coordinate parameter of the [set tile at location] block and change the direction to (bottom). Then, open Scene again and replace (location) with a (tilemap location of (sprite)) block, with the Player sprite’s name selected. This will set a crate tile at the location at the bottom of the Player sprite.


Click ▶ to see crate tiles appear underneath the Player sprite when the B button is pressed!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you drag a [set wall at] block into the [on B button pressed] container and toggle it to  <ON>?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓Why might you set a crate tile before the walls are turned on?

❓Are the walls turned on at the same location as the crate tile? How do you know?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Walk the ninja through the logic of the tilemap location blocks and how the sprite’s location is used. A crate wall tile is set at the bottom of the Player sprite’s location. Compare this to the <is sprite hitting wall [bottom]> block to show how the project uses the sprite’s location in other ways to make something happen.
steps.instructions:
The tiles were set underneath the Player sprite, but the Player sprite falls right through them! Set each crate tile as a wall so that the Player sprite can jump on top of them.


Drag a [set wall at] block inside the [on B button pressed] container and set the toggle to <ON>. Duplicate the entire (tilemap location [bottom] of (tilemap location of (sprite))) block from the [set tile at location] block and place it in the coordinate parameter of [set wall at].


Click ▶ then use the A and B buttons to set crate wall tiles underneath the Player sprite as it jumps through the air!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you drag an (otherSprite) bubble into the [destroy] block in the [on sprite overlaps sprite] container?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ How does the Player sprite collect an orb? What button needs to be pressed in order to reach orbs higher on the tilemap?

❓ Did you select a sound you like in the [play sound] block?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Remind the Ninja to use the (otherSprite) bubble from the container in the [destroy] block.

💡Encourage the Ninja to add an effect in the [destroy] block and select a matching sound in the [play sound] block. Explain to the Ninja that adding visual and sound effects improve the overall game design of a project.
steps.instructions:
Make something happen when the Player sprite collects an orb! 


Place a [destroy] block in the [on (Player) overlaps (Food)] container, then use an (otherSprite) bubble from the container as the sprite name. 


Add score to the game by placing a [set score to] block in the [on start] container, above the Player sprite’s blocks. Then, add a [change score by] block to the [on (Player) overlaps (Food)] container.


Make the project play a sound on overlap with an orb by adding a [play sound] block to the [on (Player) overlaps (Food)] container.


Click ▶ to see what happens when the Player sprite overlaps orbs on the tilemap!

steps.hints: ❓Did you use a <0=0> comparison block in the [if then] conditional to check when the score is equal to the number of orbs?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ How can you add more orbs to the tilemap to increase the score a user needs to reach to win the game?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Remind the ninja that they can update the tilemap using the editor in the [set tilemap to] block, selecting the orange spawn tile, and placing it on additional locations on the tilemap.
steps.instructions:
Allow the Player sprite to escape and win the game, once they’ve collected a certain number of orbs!


Add an [if then] conditional to the [on (Player) overlaps (Food)] container. Then, drag a <0=0> comparison block into the <true> value. Place a (score) variable in the left parameter and type the number of orbs on screen in the right parameter. 


Add a [game over] block into the conditional, then set the toggle to <WIN>. 


Click ▶ to see the Player sprite win the game once they’ve collected all of the orbs on the tilemap!

steps.hints: ❓What kind of directions would be helpful for a user of this project?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ What directions might help a user understand how to play the game?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Guide ninjas to note that while these customizing blocks are open ended and not required for the game to “work”, they really improve the Player’s experience playing a game, either by giving context to what the Player should do or not do, or to provide a more fun experience overall. They also allow the Ninja to add their personal touch and express themselves through small details present in the game.
steps.instructions:
Make the project more engaging by adding directions with a dialog box, updating the tilemap with more orbs or obstacles, or changing the background color.


Click ▶ to see the completed project!

subgroups.introduction: Create a project that uses tilemap location blocks to create wall tiles underneath the Player sprite as it jumps in the air.

validationItems.text: Add additional spawn tiles to the tilemap.
Spawn Food sprites to appear on the tilemap.
Player sprite jumps up when the A button is pressed and the bottom of the sprite is touching a tilemap wall tile.
Sprite creates a new tile when the B button is pressed. New tile is set as a wall tile.
Player sprite collects objects from the tilemap.
End the game when Player sprite collects all objects from the tilemap.
Game instructions are shared in a dialog box. Tilemap is updated with additional objects.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 4 of Green Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about tilemap location and extension blocks. These blocks can connect different tilemaps more easily and cause different things to happen based on a specific location or tile. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 4:

badges.title: Charting a Course
badges.description: Use the tilemap extension in MakeCode to extend the possibilities in a tilemap project.

badges.title: Neighbors
badges.description: Find the tilemap location next to a specific tile or sprite.

badges.title: GPS
badges.description: Find the exact tile location of a sprite on a tilemap.

badges.title: Ducks in a Row (Or Column)
badges.description: Find the row or column value of a specific location on a tilemap.

badges.title: Atlas
badges.description: Link two different tilemaps together in a project.

badges.title: Area Rug
badges.description: Temporarily cover all tiles of a specific kind on a tilemap.
